title: Sleep Staging Across the Lifespan
subtitle: What wake, N1, N2, N3 and REM look like from the premature newborn to old age, and which age-dependent findings are normal or abnormal

tabs.title: How staging works
tabs.intro: Sleep is scored in 30-second epochs, and each epoch takes the stage that fills most of it. The EEG, the eye leads (EOG) and the chin EMG are read together. The rules below follow the AASM scoring manual; the same stages apply to children from 2 months post-term, with age-adjusted features.

sections.title: The five adult stages
head: Stage
EEG
Eye leads
Chin EMG
rows: Alpha (posterior dominant rhythm) over more than half the epoch with eyes closed; with eyes open, low-voltage mixed activity
Blinks (about 0.5-2 Hz), reading or scanning movements, rapid voluntary movements
Alpha attenuated and replaced by low-amplitude mixed-frequency (4-7 Hz) activity over more than half the epoch; vertex sharp waves; in people without alpha, slowing of 1 Hz or more from wake
Usually a little lower than wake
K-complexes not linked to an arousal, or trains of sleep spindles, on a theta background
Usually none; slow eye movements may linger early
Slow waves of 0.5-2 Hz over 75 µV peak-to-peak, measured frontally, filling 20% or more of the epoch; spindles may persist
None (frontal delta can spread into the eye leads)
Low-amplitude mixed frequency like N1; sawtooth waves (2-6 Hz, central); alpha may appear 1-2 Hz slower than waking alpha
Rapid eye movements: sharp, conjugate, irregular
Lowest of the night (atonia), with brief twitches
sections.note: The older stages 3 and 4 (20-50% and over 50% delta) were combined into N3 in 2007.

sections.title: Graphoelement definitions used for scoring
head: Waveform
Definition
Where it is largest
rows: Sharply contoured wave under 0.5 s, standing out from the background
Well-delineated negative sharp wave immediately followed by a positive component, 0.5 s or more in total
Train of distinct 11-16 Hz waves (most often 12-14 Hz), 0.5 s or more
Frontal (F4-M1 is the standard measuring derivation)
Trains of sharply contoured or triangular 2-6 Hz waves, often before a burst of eye movements

cards.title: Starting N2
cards.body: Score N2 when a K-complex not associated with an arousal, or a train of spindles, appears in the first half of the epoch or the last half of the previous one.
points: A K-complex followed by an arousal does not by itself start N2
Once N2 starts, keep scoring N2 without new spindles until an arousal, a stage change, or a major body movement followed by slow eye movements and low-amplitude mixed-frequency EEG

cards.title: N3 is about amount and size
cards.body: Count the slow waves only if they exceed 75 µV peak-to-peak, measured frontally, and add up to 20% of the epoch (6 s of 30).
points: Frequency alone does not make N3
With age the waves get smaller, so fewer epochs reach the 75 µV line

cards.title: REM needs three things
cards.body: Low-voltage mixed EEG, rapid eye movements and low chin tone.
points: Rapid eye movements with normal chin tone suggest wake
REM with preserved tone is the hallmark of REM sleep behaviour disorder

cards.title: Arousal
cards.body: An abrupt shift to theta, alpha or frequencies over 16 Hz (not spindles) lasting 3 s or more after at least 10 s of stable sleep.
points: In REM an arousal also needs a rise in chin EMG for at least 1 s

sections.title: How staging changes with age (AASM)
head: Age (post-term)
States or stages scored
Key point
rows: Not covered by the AASM manual; states are scored from EEG with behaviour and polygraphy, and much of sleep is indeterminate
Infant rules: NREM is one stage (N) because spindles, K-complexes and organised slow waves are not yet reliable
Pediatric rules: the same stages as adults, scored with the dominant posterior rhythm for the child's age
Child with no spindles, K-complexes or slow waves yet
If NREM cannot be split, score the whole of it as N

sections.title: Sleep architecture by age
head: Age
REM share
Deep sleep (N3)
Cycle length
Sleep onset
rows: Slow-wave sleep develops by about 2-6 months
Highest of life; very high-voltage slow waves
Much less, sometimes almost none (men more than women)

sections.note: Typical teaching values; studies differ by a few percent. REM within 15 minutes of sleep onset (a sleep-onset REM period) is normal in young infants and abnormal in adults.

pearls: 30-second epochs; the stage filling most of the epoch wins.
N3 = 0.5-2 Hz, over 75 µV, frontal, at least 20% of the epoch.
Spindles 11-16 Hz (usually 12-14), central; K-complexes 0.5 s or more, frontal.
Infants under 2 months are scored W, N, R or T; from 2 months the adult stages apply.

tabs.title: Age groups
tabs.intro: Each card lists what you should expect in each stage at that age. Ages for the neonate are given as postmenstrual age (PMA); after that, as age after a term birth.

cards.title: Premature newborn (under 37 weeks PMA)
cards.body: States, not stages: active sleep, quiet sleep and a lot of indeterminate sleep.
points: Quiet sleep: tracé discontinu, bursts with very low-voltage gaps that shorten as PMA rises
Active sleep and wake become continuous first (by about 34 weeks)
Delta brushes (peak about 32-34 weeks) and temporal theta (about 26-32 weeks)
No spindles, vertex waves or K-complexes

cards.title: Term newborn (37-44 weeks PMA)
cards.body: Active, quiet and transitional sleep in cycles of about 50-60 minutes.
points: Sleep onset is into active sleep (REM-like): continuous low-voltage mixed activity, rapid eye movements, irregular breathing
Quiet sleep: tracé alternant (bursts alternating with lower but never flat activity) or continuous high-voltage slow activity
Frontal sharp transients and anterior dysrhythmia, mostly in transitional sleep
Tracé alternant fades by about 44-46 weeks PMA

cards.title: 1-3 months
cards.body: NREM becomes continuous slow sleep, and the first sleep transients appear.
points: Spindles first appear at about 6-8 weeks post-term: long, central, often asynchronous
Sleep onset moves from REM to NREM by about 3-4 months
A reactive occipital rhythm of about 3-4 Hz appears at 3-4 months
Under 2 months, score W, N, R, T; from 2 months, adult stages

cards.title: 3-12 months
cards.body: All the adult NREM features are now present but look different.
points: Wake: posterior rhythm about 4 Hz at 3-4 months, about 5-6 Hz by 6 months and about 6 Hz by 12 months
N1: diffuse slowing; hypnagogic hypersynchrony may begin (from about 3-6 months)
N2: vertex waves and K-complexes from about 4-6 months; spindles abundant, long and asynchronous
N3: high-voltage delta, often over 100-200 µV
REM about 30-40% of sleep

cards.title: 1-3 years
cards.body: The age of the most dramatic drowsiness.
points: Wake: posterior rhythm about 6-7 Hz at 2 years, about 8 Hz by 3 years
N1: hypnagogic hypersynchrony (bursts or runs of 3-5 Hz, often 100-300 µV) is at its most common; rhythmic anterior theta
N2: spindles should become synchronous by about 2 years; vertex waves tall and sharp
N3: very high-voltage delta

cards.title: 3-12 years (school age)
cards.body: The deepest sleep of life; vertex waves can look spiky.
points: Wake: posterior rhythm 8 Hz by 3 years, about 10 Hz by 10 years; posterior slow waves of youth
N1: hypnagogic hypersynchrony fading, usually gone by about 11-12 years
N2: vertex waves very sharp, tall and sometimes in runs; synchronous spindles; slower frontal spindles are common
N3: abundant delta, often over 200 µV
Arousal: hypnopompic hypersynchrony (rhythmic high-voltage slow activity) is normal

cards.title: Adolescence (about 12-18 years)
cards.body: Adult-like staging with less deep sleep.
points: Wake: adult alpha 9-11 Hz
N1: POSTS, 14- and 6-Hz positive bursts and other benign variants are most common now and in young adults
N2: adult spindles and K-complexes
N3: amount and amplitude fall steeply through the teens
Sleep phase shifts later (late bedtime, late waking)

cards.title: Adult (about 18-60 years)
cards.body: The reference pattern for the AASM rules.
points: N1: alpha dropout, slow rolling eye movements, vertex waves, POSTS
N2: spindles 12-14 Hz centrally, K-complexes frontally
N3: 15-20% of the night in young adults, decreasing with age
REM: about 20-25%, in 4-6 cycles; REM periods lengthen toward morning

cards.title: Older adult (over about 60 years)
cards.body: Lighter, more broken sleep with smaller transients.
points: Wake: posterior rhythm may slow slightly but should stay at 8 Hz or more
N1: more of it, and more awakenings; brief left or bilateral temporal theta in drowsiness can be age-related; wicket spikes
N2: spindles fewer, smaller and shorter; K-complexes fewer and smaller
N3: slow waves smaller, so many fail the 75 µV rule; N3 may be almost absent
REM slightly reduced; earlier bedtime and waking

tabs.eegLink: Write the patient's exact age (and PMA in infants) on the record before you comment on sleep. Almost every sleep feature is normal at one age and abnormal at another.

sections.title: Check yourself: drowsy toddler
sections.caption: NeuroLinea synthetic tracing. Drowsy 3-year-old.
sections.question: A healthy 3-year-old is drifting off to sleep when this burst appears and then settles. What is the best description?
options: Hypnagogic hypersynchrony, a normal drowsy pattern
sections.explanation: High-voltage, diffuse, rhythmic 3-5 Hz waves at sleep onset in a toddler are hypnagogic hypersynchrony, normal from about 3-6 months to about 11-12 years. There are no spikes, so it is not spike-and-wave. It is brief and tied to drowsiness, unlike encephalopathic slowing, and it is a 3-5 Hz drowsy burst in a healthy child, not the intermittent frontal delta of an encephalopathic patient.

sections.title: Check yourself: infant spindles
sections.caption: NeuroLinea synthetic tracing. Healthy 6-month-old in NREM sleep.
sections.question: In this healthy 6-month-old, spindles appear over the left and right central regions at different times. How should this be reported?
options: Abnormal asynchrony suggesting a corpus callosum defect
Abnormal: spindles should not appear before 1 year
Normal for age: spindles become synchronous by about 2 years
sections.explanation: Spindles appear at about 6-8 weeks post-term and are often asynchronous through infancy; they should be synchronous by about 2 years. Consistent absence or asymmetry on one side would be abnormal, but independent timing is not. 14- and 6-Hz positive bursts are posterior temporal and positive, in older children and adolescents.

sections.title: Things that change the picture at any age

cards.title: Drugs
cards.body: Benzodiazepines and barbiturates add beta and increase spindle-range activity while reducing deep sleep. Many antidepressants suppress REM, and stopping them can cause REM rebound.
points: Note medications on the record before staging

cards.title: Sleep deprivation
cards.body: Shortens sleep latency, deepens and increases N3 on recovery, and can bring REM early.
points: A useful activation for epileptiform discharges

cards.title: Sleep disorders
cards.body: Apnea fragments sleep with arousals; narcolepsy brings REM early; REM sleep behaviour disorder keeps chin tone in REM.
points: Add respiratory and limb channels when the history suggests them

tabs.eegLink: When you see something in sleep that looks sharp, write the age, the stage and whether it is symmetric before you call the reader.
pearls: Sleep-onset REM: normal in infants, abnormal in adults.
Asynchronous spindles: normal under about 2 years.
Hypnagogic hypersynchrony is normal in children and unusual in adults.

mistakes: N3 needs delta over more than half of the epoch.
N3 needs 0.5-2 Hz waves over 75 µV in 20% or more of the epoch; 50% was the old stage 4.
A 6-week-old without spindles has an abnormal record.
Spindles appear at about 6-8 weeks post-term, so their absence is expected this early.
Asynchronous spindles always mean a structural problem.
They are normal until about 2 years; only persistent asynchrony after that, or a consistent one-sided absence, is abnormal.
It is normal high-voltage rhythmic 3-5 Hz slowing at sleep onset in children, with no spikes.
A term newborn falling straight into REM is abnormal.
Sleep onset into active (REM-like) sleep is normal until about 3-4 months.
Older adults have the same amount of deep sleep as young adults.
Slow waves shrink with age, so N3 falls and may be almost absent.
Infants are scored with the same five stages from birth.
Under 2 months post-term the AASM infant rules use W, N, R and T.
Tall, sharp vertex waves in a child are epileptiform.
They are a normal childhood feature when symmetric, central and tied to sleep.
memory: Spindles by about 2 months; vertex waves and K-complexes by about 4-6 months
N3: over 75 µV, at least 20% of the epoch, 2 Hz or slower
Hypnagogic hypersynchrony from about 3-6 months to about 11-12 years
About 50% of newborn sleep, 25% in childhood, 20-25% in adults
